title: ML Experiment Tracking
blurb: Tests what a run has to record to be reproducible, MLflow's four parts, the model registry's lifecycle, logging and autolog, querying runs, reading a tracked sweep, and where tracking stops and data versioning or monitoring take over.

ideas.title: What a run has to record
The model registry as the promotion gate

questions.prompt: Which of these are among the six categories the chapter says a run should record? Select all that apply.
options: The git commit hash at training time
Parameters, such as max_depth
The name of the person who ran it
The dataset hash or versioned S3 path
Metrics, ideally per epoch or iteration
questions.explanation: The six are parameters, metrics, artefacts, code version, data version and environment. Missing any one breaks full reproducibility. Who ran it can be useful, but it is not in the list, and it doesn't help you reproduce the result.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter want metrics logged per epoch or iteration, not just at the end?
options: MLflow rejects a metric that has no step number.
The curve shows how training behaved, which a single final value hides.
Final values are not reproducible, but per-epoch values are.
Per-epoch logging is what lets autolog capture parameters along with the metrics.
questions.explanation: A final number says where training ended, not how it got there. Per-step values let you compare learning curves across runs. MLflow accepts metrics without a step, and per-epoch logging has nothing to do with how autolog captures parameters.

questions.prompt: Of the six categories, which does MLflow's autolog() not capture, per the chapter?
options: Metrics and artefacts
Data version and environment
Parameters and metrics
Artefacts and code version
questions.explanation: The chapter says autolog() captures the first four: parameters, metrics, artefacts and code version. Data versioning is handled separately, which Chapter 24 covers. The environment is the sixth category, outside autolog's four.

questions.prompt: A run logs parameters, metrics, the model file and the git commit, but not the Python and library versions. A year later, rerunning the same commit on the same data gives a different score. What was missing?
options: The run name. MLflow needs it to restore the original random seeds.
The environment. A library upgrade can change results even with identical code and data.
The data version. A git commit hash also fixes the data, so the data must have changed.
Nothing. Small run-to-run differences are expected, and the run is still fully reproducible.
questions.explanation: The environment (Python and library versions) is one of the six categories. Missing any one breaks full reproducibility. The data was the same here, and a git hash does not pin the data anyway. A run name is a label, not a seed store.

questions.prompt: Which MLflow component is the packaging convention, an MLproject file naming entry point, parameters and environment?
options: Model Registry
Tracking
Projects
Models
questions.explanation: Projects packages code so it runs reproducibly on any machine. Tracking is the logging layer. Models is a standard save format. The Model Registry is the catalogue with a lifecycle.

questions.prompt: A team saved one model from sklearn and another from PyTorch, both in MLflow's Models format. How do they load them?
options: Through the Model Registry only, because the Models format cannot be loaded directly
By rerunning the training run that produced each one
The same way for both, with mlflow.pyfunc.load_model()
With each framework's own loader, since MLflow only stores the files
questions.explanation: The point of the Models format is that any model saved with it loads back through mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(), whatever framework built it. That makes serving code framework-neutral. Neither registration nor retraining is needed to load it.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter describe the relationship between experiments and runs in MLflow Tracking?
options: Experiments and runs are two names for the same thing.
Every experiment lives inside a run, which groups related experiments.
Every run lives inside an experiment, which is a logical grouping of runs.
An experiment is a registered model, and each run is one of that model's versions.
questions.explanation: An experiment groups runs, and each run carries its parameters, metrics and artefacts. That is why set_experiment comes before start_run in Listing 22.1. Model versions belong to the registry, not to experiments.

questions.prompt: What is the model registry's lifecycle, in order?
options: None, Staging, Production, Archived
Draft, Review, Production, Retired
Candidate, Production, Staging, Archived
Staging, None, Production, Archived
questions.explanation: The chapter gives None → Staging → Production → Archived. A newly registered version starts at None, is promoted to Staging for checks, then Production, then Archived when replaced.

questions.prompt: Which question is the model registry built to answer?
options: How much did the last training run cost?
Has the live data drifted since the model was trained?
Which model is in production right now, and which run produced it?
Which hyperparameters give the best score on this dataset?
questions.explanation: The registry is the promotion gate between experimentation and deployment, with an auditable trail from the production model back to its run. Finding the best hyperparameters is a tracking query. Drift is a monitoring question.

questions.prompt: In Listing 22.5, what does the model_uri runs:/{best_run_id}/model point to?
options: The MLproject file that was used to package and train the model
The model's current production endpoint
The model artefact logged inside a specific tracking run
A model version already in the registry
questions.explanation: A runs:/ URI names an artefact path inside a run. register_model takes that artefact and creates a new registry version from it. It does not point at a registry version, an endpoint or a project file.

questions.prompt: Right after the two calls in Listing 22.5, where does the new model version stand?
options: Archived, because each registration archives itself until reviewed
In Staging, because transition_model_version_stage moved it there
In Production, because registering a model promotes it automatically
In None, because transitions only take effect after the next run
questions.explanation: register_model creates the version, and the next call transitions it to stage="Staging". Promotion to Production is a separate, explicit step. That is the point of the registry as a gate.

questions.prompt: The chapter's mental model compares tracking to git. Which mapping does it give, and what does it imply for a model nobody has reviewed?
options: Each artefact is a commit and the registry is the remote. An unreviewed model is pushed when the run ends.
Each experiment is a repository and the registry is a tag. An unreviewed model can go to production if it scores best.
Each run is a branch and the registry is a pull request. An unreviewed model is merged automatically as soon as its run finishes.
Each run is a commit and the registry is the main branch. An unreviewed model stays a candidate until someone promotes it.
questions.explanation: The chapter says every run should be a commit, and the registry is the main branch where only promoted, reviewed models live. Everything else stays a candidate until someone explicitly says otherwise. The best score alone does not promote a model, and nothing is promoted automatically.

questions.prompt: Procedure 22.3 says to turn autolog off after a sweep. What goes wrong if you leave it on?
options: It raises an error on the next call to fit.
It overwrites the parameters of the runs already logged.
It logs every later training call as a run, cluttering the experiment.
It stops logging metrics for later runs but keeps logging their parameters.
questions.explanation: The chapter's common mistake: autolog stays active and logs every subsequent training call as a run. It does not overwrite earlier runs, drop metrics, or raise errors. The harm is clutter, which makes the experiment harder to read.

questions.prompt: Where in the script does Listing 22.3 call mlflow.sklearn.autolog()?
options: Inside the predict call, so it captures test metrics
After disabling it, to flush the logs
Before creating and fitting the model
After fitting, so it can read the trained model
questions.explanation: The listing's comment says to enable it before creating the model, so the fit call is captured. Calling it after fit is too late for that run.

questions.prompt: In Listing 22.4, runs = mlflow.search_runs(experiment_names=[...], order_by=["metrics.f1 DESC"]). What does runs.iloc[0]['run_id'] hold?
options: The run ID with the highest F1 in that experiment
The run ID with the lowest F1, since iloc[0] is the first logged run
The most recent run, whatever its F1
The run currently in Production in the registry
questions.explanation: search_runs returns a DataFrame. Ordering by metrics.f1 DESC puts the highest F1 first, so row 0 is the best run. The query knows nothing about registry stages.

questions.prompt: A team logs a training loss on every batch in a loop that runs each batch in a few milliseconds. Training slows down. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Switch to autolog, which logs every batch with no overhead.
Log to a remote server instead, which removes the overhead.
Stop tracking that model. Tracking is only worth doing for slow training jobs.
Log less often. Each call has a small overhead that adds up quickly in tight loops.
questions.explanation: The trade-offs section says logging adds a small overhead per call, so per-batch logging at millisecond scale has to be selective about frequency. Dropping tracking loses far more. Neither autolog nor a remote server removes the per-call cost.

questions.prompt: The worked example sweeps n_estimators over {50, 200} and max_depth over {3, 6}. How many runs does the grid make?
questions.explanation: Two values times two values gives 2 × 2 = 4 configurations, each logged as its own run.

questions.prompt: Which configurations tie for the best F1 (0.9655) in the worked example?
options: Only 200 trees at depth 6
50 trees at depth 6, and 200 trees at depth 3
200 trees at depth 6, and 200 trees at depth 3
50 trees at depth 3, and 200 trees at depth 6
questions.explanation: The measured results are 0.9583 for 50/3, 0.9655 for 50/6, 0.9655 for 200/3 and 0.9583 for 200/6. The largest model, 200 trees at depth 6, is among the lower pair.

questions.prompt: What lesson does the chapter draw from the sweep's results?
options: Tree count alone doesn't explain the ranking, which you only learn by tracking the runs.
The results are noise, so tracking a sweep of four runs gives no information.
Depth matters and tree count doesn't, so tree count can always be set to the minimum tried.
More trees always helps, so the largest configuration should go to production.
questions.explanation: 50 trees at depth 6 matched 200 trees at depth 3 exactly, and 200 at depth 6 scored lower. So neither "more trees" nor "deeper" alone explains it. The chapter's point is that you find this from tracked results rather than assume it. Four runs say nothing about tree count being irrelevant in general.

questions.prompt: Two configurations tie on F1. One uses 200 trees, the other 50. You have to pick one for production and you care about inference cost. What does the tracked sweep let you do?
options: Pick the 200-tree run, because a tie should always go to the larger model.
Rerun the whole sweep first, because tracked results alone can't be trusted for a production decision.
Pick the 50-tree run, register it with its logged parameters, and keep the comparison on record.
Pick either. A tie means the two models are identical in every way that matters.
questions.explanation: The tie is on one metric, not on cost. Fewer trees means cheaper inference, so the 50-tree run is the natural pick, and tracking keeps its exact parameters and lineage for the registry. The two models are not identical, and a tie gives no reason to prefer the larger one.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter separate experiment tracking from monitoring?
options: Tracking watches training. Monitoring watches the live model serving traffic.
Monitoring records hyperparameters during training. Tracking records serving latency.
Tracking replaces monitoring once a model is registered.
Tracking is for deep learning. Monitoring is for classical ML.
questions.explanation: Tracking covers what happened while building the model. Monitoring covers what happens while it serves. The chapter says both are needed and neither substitutes for the other.

questions.prompt: A run logged its data path, s3://bucket/train.csv. Someone later overwrote that file. What can MLflow tell you?
options: Only the path used. It can't see that the data there changed, so you need DVC or S3 versioning.
The original data, because MLflow copies every input file into the run.
Nothing, because MLflow does not record data paths at all.
That the file changed, because MLflow re-hashes every logged path each time you query it.
questions.explanation: The trade-offs section says tracking records which data path was used, not whether the data there later changed. DVC or S3 versioning covers that. MLflow does not copy or re-hash input files.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter still make MLflow the default over Weights & Biases for most enterprise work?
options: MLflow is better at deep learning than W&B.
W&B cannot log metrics per epoch.
W&B has no hosted dashboard, so teams must run and patch their own server.
It is open source, runs on any infrastructure, and SageMaker hosts it.
questions.explanation: The chapter names those three reasons. W&B is the main alternative, with a deep-learning focus and a hosted dashboard, which is the reverse of the third and fourth options. Per-epoch logging is not mentioned as a W&B gap.

bookExercises.prompt: List the six categories of information needed for full reproducibility of a training run, and state which of the six MLflow's `autolog()` does NOT capture automatically.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The six categories: parameters, metrics, artefacts, code version, data version, environment. `autolog()` does NOT automatically capture data version (which dataset/path/hash was used). That has to be logged explicitly (e.g. via a manually set tag), or handled through a separate data-versioning tool like DVC.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain the difference between MLflow Tracking and the MLflow Model Registry in one or two sentences.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Tracking is the logging layer recording every run's parameters, metrics, and artefacts as they happen, for comparison and reproducibility. The Model Registry is a separate, curated catalogue sitting on top of tracking, holding only models that have been explicitly promoted through a lifecycle (Staging → Production → Archived). Tracking records everything tried. The registry records what's actually deployed.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 22.6's measured results, explain why `n_estimators=200, max_depth=6` (0.9583) scored *lower* than `n_estimators=50, max_depth=6` (0.9655) despite using 4x more trees at the same depth. What does this suggest about this configuration relative to the dataset's actual complexity?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: This suggests the dataset's real complexity is well captured by a moderately deep, moderately-sized forest (50 trees at depth 6), and that adding more trees at the same depth (200 vs. 50) didn't help. On this specific train/test split, it landed marginally worse, likely from ordinary variance in how the additional trees' bootstrap samples happened to vote, not because more trees are inherently worse. It's a reminder that "more trees" isn't a free accuracy improvement past the point where the ensemble has already stabilised, exactly the point Chapter 12's ensemble methods chapter makes about bagging's variance reduction saturating.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 22.7's pattern, write a `filter_string` for `mlflow.search_runs` that would return only runs with `max_depth=6` and F1 above 0.96, and state which of this chapter's four logged runs would match.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `filter_string="params.max_depth = '6' and metrics.f1 > 0.96"`. Of this chapter's four logged runs, only `n_estimators=50, max_depth=6` (F1=0.9655) matches both conditions. The other `max_depth=6` run (`n_estimators=200`) scored 0.9583, below the 0.96 threshold.

bookExercises.prompt: A team says "we don't need MLflow, we just name our output files carefully like `model_v3_final_FINAL.pkl`." Using this chapter's Motivation section, write the two or three sentences you'd say about what that convention doesn't solve.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Careful filenames still leave you unable to answer which exact hyperparameters, code version, and data produced `model_v3_final_FINAL.pkl` six months later, or to compare it against the twelve other configurations that were tried but never saved. Naming conventions capture a label, not the reproducible record of parameters, metrics, and environment that tracking captures automatically and queryably."

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague enables `mlflow.sklearn.autolog()` at the top of a long notebook and never disables it. Using this chapter's Troubleshooting guidance, predict what will go wrong by the end of the session.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Every subsequent `.fit()` call in the notebook, including exploratory ones never meant to be "real" experiments, will get silently logged as its own MLflow run. That clutters the experiment with dozens of unintended entries, making it harder to find the runs that actually mattered: exactly the failure mode this chapter's Troubleshooting table names directly.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the MLflow documentation's description of the Model Registry stage transition API. Identify what `archive_existing_versions=True` does when promoting a new version to Production, and explain why that default matters for the registry's "which model is in production right now" guarantee.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. `archive_existing_versions=True` automatically moves whatever model version currently holds the "Production" stage to "Archived" at the moment a new version is promoted into "Production". Without it, two versions could simultaneously claim the Production stage, breaking the registry's core guarantee of being able to answer "which model is in production right now" with a single, unambiguous answer.
